name: Beauty privilege research (pretty premium)

lead: The pretty premium is the research finding that people rated more attractive tend to be hired more and paid more. Looksmaxxers cite it as a reason to invest in appearance. The landmark 1993 to 1994 study by Hamermesh and Biddle reported a plainness penalty of about 5 to 10 percent in earnings, somewhat larger than the beauty premium.

The chain: higher rated attractiveness, better hiring and pay outcomes, motivation to improve looks. Later résumé experiments in Argentina, Israel and Peru found callback advantages for attractive applicants, with patterns that differ by country and sex. Researchers propose halo-effect bias, employer or customer preferences, and productivity in interpersonal jobs; which applies is debated.

paras: People use it as a reason to prioritise grooming, fitness, skincare and style, particularly for interviews and customer-facing work. It is a body of findings rather than a practice.

No direct physical risk. Studies are observational or résumé experiments and do not show that specific looks changes raise earnings. Some jurisdictions, such as Belgium, have laws covering appearance-based discrimination.

web.title: Beauty and the Labor Market - NBER
Beauty Impacts Hiring, Salaries and Profits, Economist Finds - UT Austin

angle.text: Looksmaxxers cite labour-economics findings that more attractive people tend to get better hiring and pay outcomes as a reason to invest in appearance. The premium is documented in research, while its size and causes are still debated.

lead: The pretty premium, or beauty premium, is the research finding that people rated as more physically attractive tend to receive better outcomes in hiring and pay than people rated as less attractive. For people working on their appearance it supplies a concrete reason to invest in grooming, skin, fitness and style: the studies describe measurable payoffs in jobs and income for how someone looks. Popular and online usage calls it 'pretty privilege' or 'lookism'. [1][2]

The best-known early study is the 1993 to 1994 paper 'Beauty and the Labor Market' by Daniel Hamermesh and Jeff Biddle, which used US and Canadian surveys in which interviewers rated respondents' appearance. They reported that plain-looking people earned less than average-looking people, who earned less than good-looking people, with a plainness penalty of about 5 to 10 percent, somewhat larger than the beauty premium, and with effects somewhat larger for men than for women. [2]

Later field experiments sent fictitious resumes with photographs and compared callbacks, with mixed patterns by country and sex. Researchers also dispute how the results should be interpreted, and some authors argue that appearance preferences may reflect evolved tendencies or productivity rather than injustice. [1] Hamermesh's 2011 book Beauty Pays summarised the field, and university coverage reported that the best-looking third of workers earned about 5 percent more than average-looking colleagues and 10 to 12 percent more than the least attractive. [3][4]

In looksmaxxing culture the literature is cited as a rationale for working on appearance, alongside discussion of dating outcomes. The studies measure rated attractiveness; they do not test whether particular grooming, skincare or fitness changes alter earnings. [5][6]

paras: Lookism is defined as prejudice or discrimination against people considered physically unattractive, and the opposite is sometimes called 'pretty privilege' or 'body privilege'. The term grew popular in the 1970s within the fat acceptance movement, and The Washington Post used it in 1978. [1] Smith College used the word in the 1990s to warn incoming students about it. [1] Psychologist Nancy Etcoff has described lookism as one of the most pervasive but denied prejudices. [1]

Research on the topic spans wages, hiring, dating, education, politics and legal settings. A common thread is the 'halo effect', the tendency to attribute positive traits such as intelligence and honesty to attractive people. [7][8] Researchers who study it generally measure attractiveness through ratings: survey interviewers or panels of raters score photos or in-person appearance, and economists then compare outcomes across rating groups while controlling for education, experience and other characteristics. [2][3]

Hamermesh has said that raters broadly agree on who is good-looking, and in his words beauty is scarce in economic terms. [3] That agreement is what lets researchers treat a rating as a measurable trait rather than a matter of private taste.

The psychological roots lie in the halo effect. Frederick Wells is credited with identifying it in 1907, and Edward Thorndike named it in 1920 after finding that officers' ratings of soldiers on separate traits correlated suspiciously highly. [8] Solomon Asch's 1946 work on 'warm' and 'cold' labels showed how one impression colours others. [8]

Applied to looks, Dion, Berscheid and Walster (1972) asked 60 University of Minnesota students to judge photos of attractive, average and unattractive people. Attractive people were assumed to have more desirable traits, happier lives and more career success, though they were judged to be worse parents. [8] In 1974 Landy and Sigall found that identical essays were graded higher when attributed to attractive female authors, with the largest gap for the poorly written essay. [8]

Economists entered the field in the early 1990s. Daniel Hamermesh, a labour economist at the University of Texas at Austin, and Jeff Biddle issued 'Beauty and the Labor Market' as NBER Working Paper 4518 in November 1993; it appeared in the American Economic Review in December 1994. [2] Hamermesh later wrote Beauty Pays (Princeton University Press, 2011) for a general audience. [3][4]

Hamermesh and Biddle drew on three surveys: a 1977 Quality of Employment survey, a 1971 Quality of American Life survey and a 1981 Canadian Quality of Life survey, each including interviewer ratings of appearance. Controlling for demographic and labour-market characteristics, plain-looking workers earned less than average-looking workers, who earned less than good-looking workers. The plainness penalty, about 5 to 10 percent, was somewhat larger than the beauty premium, and effects were slightly larger for men than for women. [2]

They also reported that unattractive women were less likely to participate in the labour force and more likely to be married to men with unexpectedly low human capital. Better-looking people tended to enter occupations where looks are likely to matter more for productivity, but the effect of looks on earnings was largely the same across occupations. [2]

In his 2011 summary, Hamermesh reported that the most attractive people earn roughly 250,000 dollars more over a career than the least attractive, and that after adjusting for education and other factors the top third in looks earns about 5 percent more than average-looking people and 10 to 12 percent more than the least attractive. He added that looks affect men's earnings more than women's, which he partly attributed to women having more options to leave the workforce, that attractive women tend to marry higher-earning men, and that better-looking people report being happier. [3] Other authors cited a 7 to 9 percent penalty for the bottom 9 percent in looks and a 5 percent premium for the top third. [1]

A study of American football quarterbacks reported a positive correlation between facial symmetry and salary (Berri, 2008). [7] Stinebrickner and co-authors reported in 2019 that the premium depends on how much a job involves interpersonal interaction. [1]

Field experiments send fictitious resumes with photographs in reply to real job advertisements and count callbacks. In Argentina, 2,540 resumes were sent and attractive applicants received 36 percent more callbacks. [1] In Israel, 5,312 resumes went to 2,656 openings; attractive men received more callbacks, while the advantage did not hold for women, and women without photos received higher callback rates. [1] In Peru, 4,899 resumes went to 1,247 openings: attractive applicants received 82 percent more interview callbacks, applicants with White-associated surnames received 54 percent more than those with Quechua-associated surnames, and men received 34 percent more than women. [1]
The varied patterns by country, sex and job type are part of why researchers describe the premium as context-dependent rather than a single fixed number. [1]

Efran (1974) found more lenient sentencing of attractive defendants and Sigall and Ostrove (1975) found the pattern reversed when the offence itself involved attractiveness, such as a swindle. [8] A 2010 study reported that one-second exposures to photos of congressional candidates were reasonably predictive of election outcomes. [8] Studies in several countries have reported that attractive political candidates gain more votes. [1]

A 2023 study of 2,748 participants, published in 2024, found that people rated the same faces higher on intelligence, trustworthiness, sociability and happiness after beauty filters were applied. [8] Murphy, Jako and Anhalt (1993) argued, on the other side, that halo effects are not always harmful and can sometimes improve rating accuracy. [8]

A 2010 OkCupid analysis of about 200,000 users found that male desirability to women peaks in the late 20s, while female desirability to men peaks at 21. [7] Dan Ariely, cited by journalist Lori Gottlieb in 2010, reported that a 5 foot 4 inch man would need about 229,000 dollars more income than a 6 foot man to be equally appealing to American women. [1] Hamermesh's own work reports that attractive women tend to marry higher-earning men. [3]
No clinical trials were found; the evidence comes from observational labour-market surveys, field experiments and laboratory studies in economics and psychology, summarised above. [2][1]

Researchers offer several explanations for the premium: employer or customer preferences, halo-effect bias, and real productivity differences in jobs that involve interpersonal contact. Which applies is debated. [1][2]

Tietje and Cresap, in a 2005 paper titled 'Is Lookism Unjust?', argued that appearance judgments may be a biological adaptation, that attractiveness can be job-relevant when it raises company performance, and that policies to redress beauty discrimination would be impractical to justify. [1] Nancy Etcoff argues that the preference for attractiveness is rooted in evolution, that preventing it from influencing people is unrealistic, and that being prized for beauty is not a social evil. [1]

Hamermesh himself calls judging people by looks silly but describes the attitudes as an economic reality that firms respond to. He suggests that people who are not rated as good-looking can compete on other traits, citing comparative advantage. [3] The Wikipedia article on lookism notes that the topic has received less cultural attention and fewer legal protections than racism or sexism, and that its coverage focuses mainly on the United States. [1]

In the United States, 'ugly laws' barred people with unsightly disfigurements from appearing in public in many jurisdictions until the 1970s. Today a few cities protect against appearance-based discrimination, there is no federal law covering appearance, and the EEOC treats extreme obesity as a disability under the Americans with Disabilities Act. [1] Belgium's Anti-Discrimination Law of 10 May 2007 prohibits discrimination based on physical or genetic characteristics. [1]

Adjacent terms include heightism, colorism, texturism, fatphobia and cacophobia, along with the physical attractiveness stereotype and the 'horn effect', where one negative trait colours overall judgment. Writers on the subject also describe intersectionality, in which appearance interacts with race, gender, class and age. [1][8]

In looksmaxxing communities the beauty-premium literature is invoked as an economic and social rationale for changing appearance. A looksmax.org thread titled 'Lookism Awareness: What Now?' asks members whether knowing how large a role looks play in how people are treated changes how they treat attractive or unattractive people. [5] Another thread title asserts that lookism theory and the halo effect are real. [6]
The studies themselves measure rated attractiveness and do not test whether specific appearance interventions change earnings. [2][3]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, lookism is discussed as a fact of how people are treated, and posters debate whether it should change how they treat others or whether it makes appearance improvement essential. [5][6]

claims.claim: Looks strongly determine how people are treated, so improving appearance pays off.
The halo effect, attributing good traits to attractive people, is real.
Looks matter more for men's pay than women's.
People who are not rated as good-looking can make up the difference with other traits.
Favouring attractive people is a natural tendency and not an injustice.
Attractive people get more lenient treatment in courts and politics.
